It recovers the signal well: both blocks come back with sharp edges in the right places and almost the right heights, and the error is about half that of the simpler methods I compared it against.\n\n## Why I chose this method\n- **Your operator:** a 200×200 Gaussian blur. Its condition number is about 1.8e14, so it can't be inverted directly without blowing up the noise; the inversion needs regularisation. It passed `dottest` (a standard check that its adjoint is correct).\n- **Your signal:** made of flat blocks with sharp jumps. That calls for **total variation (TV) regularisation**, which penalises the size of the jumps and so favours flat pieces. I solved it with `pylops.splitbregman` using an L1 penalty on `FirstDerivative`, with `mu=0.01` and TV weight `eps=0.05`. The run did 100 outer × 5 inner iterations.\n- **Two simpler methods for comparison:** damped `lsqr` (`damp=0.05`) and a smoothness penalty on the second derivative (`regularized_inversion`, `eps=1`). Both penalise squared values rather than jumps.\n\n## Results (noise σ = 0.02, which corresponds to a relative residual of about 0.041)\n\n| Method | Data residual ‖y−Ax‖/‖y‖ | Model error ‖x−xtrue‖/‖xtrue‖ | SNR |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| lsqr (damped) | 0.036 | 0.176 | 15.1 dB |\n| Smoothness penalty | 0.038 | 0.190 | 14.4 dB |\n| **TV (Split Bregman)** | **0.045** | **0.100** | **20.0 dB** |\n\n- **TV result:** the edges are sharp and in the right places. The flat parts are clean: the zero sections vary by only about 0.002. The block heights come out at 0.987 (true value 1.0) and −0.668 (true value −0.7). TV always shrinks heights slightly like this.\n- **The two simpler methods** blur the edges and leave ripples in the flat parts. Their residuals are slightly below the noise level, so they are fitting some of the noise. The TV residual is slightly above it (0.045 vs 0.041), so it is a touch over-regularised.\n- **Convergence:** the TV run used all 100 outer iterations without hitting the `tol` stop. The cost dropped quickly over the first ~10 iterations and changed by only about 0.1% over the last 50. The model has effectively stopped changing, so more iterations wouldn't help.\n\n## Files (in the current directory)\n- `invert_blur.py`: the script. Run it with `python invert_blur.py`.\n- `invert_blur.npz`: data, the three recovered signals and the TV cost history.\n- `invert_blur.png`: data with fit and residual, the recovered signals against the true one, and the cost curve.\n\n## Next step\nThe regularisation weights (`eps_tv`, `mu`, `damp`, `eps_l2`) were set by order-of-magnitude reasoning and haven't been tuned. Because the residual is slightly above the noise level, `eps_tv` is probably a bit too large. Lowering it a little should bring the residual down to the noise level and restore some of the block height. {"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Base directory for this skill: /Users/mrava87/Desktop/OpenSource/pylops-agent-skills/plugins/pylops/skills/solve-inverse-problem\n\nGoal: a **runnable, reproducible inversion script** in the user's project that\nsolves their problem with a solver and regularisation chosen for a stated reason,\nand shows whether it converged. Do not modify the installed `pylops` package.\n\nIf the user has no operator yet, use the `wrap-operator` skill first. If they\nalready have an inversion that misbehaves, use `debug-inversion` instead. To\nchoose regularisation weights, hand over to `tune-regularization` once the setup\nbelow works.\n\n## 0. Check the environment\n\n- Find how the project runs Python (`uv.lock`, `pyproject.toml`,\n  `environment.yml`, `requirements*.txt`, active venv) and use that runner.\n- Check PyLops and its version: `python -c \"import pylops; print(pylops.__version__)\"`.\n  Solver signatures and return tuples changed across versions: inspect the\n  installed ones (`help(pylops.optimization.basic.cgls)`) rather than trusting\n  memory. `reference/solver_guide.md` describes PyLops 2.x.\n- Optional packages: `spgl1` is needed by `pylops.optimization.sparsity.spgl1`;\n  PyProximal is needed for non-smooth problems beyond what PyLops offers. Ask\n  before installing anything.\n\n## 1. Characterise the problem\n\nBefore picking a solver, write down (and confirm with the user if unclear):\n\n- `Op.shape = (N, M)`, `Op.dims`, `Op.dimsd`, dtype (real/complex);\n- whether the problem is **square/symmetric positive definite** (e.g. already\n  normal equations), **overdetermined** (`N > M`), or **underdetermined**\n  (`N < M`, e.g. interpolation, compressive sensing);\n- the **noise** level (known sigma? SNR?) and whether data are available on a\n  subset only (then the operator should include a `Restriction`);\n- the **prior** the user expects on the model: smooth, blocky/piecewise\n  constant, sparse in some transform, bounded, positive, low-rank;\n- the size: can `Op.todense()` be afforded for a sanity check (M, N up to a few\n  thousand)?\n\nRun `pylops.utils.dottest(Op, *Op.shape, complexflag=...)` once. If it fails,\nstop and switch to `debug-inversion` / `wrap-operator`: no solver will fix a wrong\nadjoint.\n\n## 2. Pick the solver\n\nUse `reference/solver_guide.md` for the full decision table and return values.\nIn short:\n\n| Prior / structure | Start with |\n|---|---|\n| well-posed, overdetermined, no prior | `lsqr` or `cgls` (`damp` for zero-order Tikhonov) |\n| symmetric positive (semi)definite `Op` | `cg` |\n| smooth model | `regularized_inversion` with `Regs=[SecondDerivative/Laplacian]`, `epsRs=[...]` |\n| model best expressed in another basis | `preconditioned_inversion` with `P` (e.g. smoothing or a synthesis transform) |\n| sparse in the model or in a transform `T` (signal → coefficients) | `fista` (`SOp=T.H`) or `spgl1` (`SOp=T`, note the opposite convention) if a residual target `sigma` is known – see `pick-sparsifying-transform` |\n| few non-zeros, explicit dictionary | `omp` |\n| robust to outliers (L1 data misfit) | `irls` with `kind=\"data\"` |\n| blocky / TV-like, mixed L1 + L2 terms | `splitbregman` with `RegsL1=[FirstDerivative/Gradient]` |\n| constraints (bounds, positivity), TV with better control, other non-smooth terms | PyProximal: use the `pyproximal` plugin skill `solve-nonsmooth-problem` |\n\nAvoid `Op / y` in production code: it is a convenience wrapper with a fixed\n100 iterations and no control over stopping or regularisation.\n\nState which solver was picked and why (one or two sentences) before writing code.\n\n## 3. Write the script\n\nStart from `reference/inversion_template.py` and adapt it:\n\n- build (or import) the operator, load the data, reshape to `Op.dimsd`;\n- **scale** data and model sensibly: if `|y|` is ~1e-8 or ~1e8 normalise it and\n  undo the scaling on the result; badly scaled problems stall Krylov solvers;\n- set `x0` (zero, or a smooth background model when the user has one);\n- choose `niter` from the problem size and condition, not \"1000 to be safe\":\n  start with 20–100 for Krylov solvers and 100–500 for (F)ISTA, then look at the\n  cost curve. Use `tol` / `rtol` to stop early;\n- for regularised solvers, set initial weights from a scale argument\n  (e.g. `eps ≈ ||Op.H y|| / ||Reg.H Reg x||` order-of-magnitude) and mark them as\n  \"to be tuned\" – do not claim they are optimal;\n- for `fista`/`ista`, let `alpha=None` so PyLops estimates the step from the\n  largest eigenvalue, or pass `eigsdict={\"niter\": ..., \"tol\": ...}` for big\n  operators; `eps` is the threshold weight;\n- keep the whole solver return tuple and name its entries (they differ between\n  solvers – see `reference/solver_guide.md`);\n- save outputs (`np.save` / the project's I/O) rather than only plotting.\n\nPut the script where the user keeps analysis code (ask if ambiguous) and use\nthe project's plotting conventions if any.\n\n## 4. Check the result\n\nRun the script and report, with numbers:\n\n- solver exit status (`istop` where available) and iterations used;\n- the **cost curve** (log scale) – flat from iteration 1 means a wrong setup,\n  still decreasing at `niter` means increase it;\n- data residual `||y - Op x|| / ||y||` compared with the expected noise level\n  (much lower than the noise ⇒ overfitting; much higher ⇒ under-fitting or\n  a modelling error);\n- if the user has a true model (synthetic), `pylops.utils.metrics.snr(xtrue, xinv)`;\n- a plot of the model (and data, modelled data, residual).\n\nIf something looks wrong, switch to `debug-inversion` rather than randomly\nchanging parameters.\n\n## 5. Hand off\n\nReport: the solver and regularisation chosen and why, the file path, the\nconvergence summary above, and the parameters that should be tuned next\n(pointing to `tune-regularization`).\n"}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"6a476a17-b2bf-4667-89be-47e81b3f5c16","uuid":"7a492ef1-a4e1-4e57-b3b7-28bc7d45738a","timestamp":"2026-11-01T21:11:34.078Z","isSynthetic":true}

It recovers your signal well: an SNR of **31.1 dB** against the true model, with the edges in the right places and flat plateaus at the correct heights.\n\n**What the script does**\n1. **Checks the operator.** It builds your operator and data exactly as you gave them, then runs PyLops' adjoint check (`dottest`), which passed. The operator is 200×200, but its condition number is about 1.8e14: the blur removes high frequencies almost completely, so some regularisation is required.\n2. **Main inversion.** It uses Split-Bregman with a TV penalty. TV penalises the jumps between neighbouring samples, which suits a signal made of flat segments with sharp edges. Settings: `mu=1.0`, TV weight `epsRL1s=[0.1]`, 100 outer × 5 inner iterations, and 30 LSQR iterations per inner step.\n3. **Two baselines for comparison.** One is plain unregularised LSQR. The other is a smooth inversion (`regularized_inversion` with a second-derivative penalty, weight 0.5).\n4. **Outputs.** It saves `invert_blur_results.npz` (all the models, the data and the cost history) and `invert_blur.png` (data with fit and residual, the models, and the cost curve).\n\n**Results**\n\n| Method | Relative data residual | SNR vs. true model |\n|---|---|---|\n| LSQR, no regularisation | 3.29e-2 | −19.9 dB (noise blows up) |\n| Smooth (second derivative) | 3.65e-2 | 14.8 dB (wiggles and overshoot at the edges) |\n| **TV Split-Bregman** | **3.70e-2** | **31.1 dB** |\n\nThe noise alone would give a relative residual of about 4.09e-2. All the residuals are below that, so none of the methods underfit the data.\n\n**One adjustment, and what's still open**\n- **The TV weight.** My first value, 0.02, gave only 18 dB. Its residual was further below the noise level, and the model had small false steps around z≈170–190, so it was fitting noise. A quick check showed SNR rising with the weight: 0.05 → 23 dB, 0.1 → 31 dB, 0.2 → 33 dB. I set 0.1. Even 0.2 keeps the residual below the noise level, so pushing towards the residual-equals-noise target would raise the weight further. Treat 0.1 as a good starting point, not an optimum. Picking the weight by SNR only works here because you know the true signal; on real data, raise the weight until the residual roughly matches the noise level.\n- **Convergence.** The cost curve levels off after about 30–40 outer iterations. The stopping tolerance was never reached, so the solver ran all 100. Cutting to around 40 would give nearly the same result, faster.\n- **Next step.** Tune the TV weight properly, and `mu` with it, with a residual-vs-noise or L-curve sweep. {"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Base directory for this skill: /Users/mrava87/Desktop/OpenSource/pylops-agent-skills/plugins/pylops/skills/solve-inverse-problem\n\nGoal: a **runnable, reproducible inversion script** in the user's project that\nsolves their problem with a solver and regularisation chosen for a stated reason,\nand shows whether it converged. Do not modify the installed `pylops` package.\n\nIf the user has no operator yet, use the `wrap-operator` skill first. If they\nalready have an inversion that misbehaves, use `debug-inversion` instead. To\nchoose regularisation weights, hand over to `tune-regularization` once the setup\nbelow works.\n\n## 0. Check the environment\n\n- Find how the project runs Python (`uv.lock`, `pyproject.toml`,\n  `environment.yml`, `requirements*.txt`, active venv) and use that runner.\n- Check PyLops and its version: `python -c \"import pylops; print(pylops.__version__)\"`.\n  Solver signatures and return tuples changed across versions: inspect the\n  installed ones (`help(pylops.optimization.basic.cgls)`) rather than trusting\n  memory. `reference/solver_guide.md` describes PyLops 2.x.\n- Optional packages: `spgl1` is needed by `pylops.optimization.sparsity.spgl1`;\n  PyProximal is needed for non-smooth problems beyond what PyLops offers. Ask\n  before installing anything.\n\n## 1. Characterise the problem\n\nBefore picking a solver, write down (and confirm with the user if unclear):\n\n- `Op.shape = (N, M)`, `Op.dims`, `Op.dimsd`, dtype (real/complex);\n- whether the problem is **square/symmetric positive definite** (e.g. already\n  normal equations), **overdetermined** (`N > M`), or **underdetermined**\n  (`N < M`, e.g. interpolation, compressive sensing);\n- the **noise** level (known sigma? SNR?) and whether data are available on a\n  subset only (then the operator should include a `Restriction`);\n- the **prior** the user expects on the model: smooth, blocky/piecewise\n  constant, sparse in some transform, bounded, positive, low-rank;\n- the size: can `Op.todense()` be afforded for a sanity check (M, N up to a few\n  thousand)?\n\nRun `pylops.utils.dottest(Op, *Op.shape, complexflag=...)` once. If it fails,\nstop and switch to `debug-inversion` / `wrap-operator`: no solver will fix a wrong\nadjoint.\n\n## 2. Pick the solver\n\nUse `reference/solver_guide.md` for the full decision table and return values.\nIn short:\n\n| Prior / structure | Start with |\n|---|---|\n| well-posed, overdetermined, no prior | `lsqr` or `cgls` (`damp` for zero-order Tikhonov) |\n| symmetric positive (semi)definite `Op` | `cg` |\n| smooth model | `regularized_inversion` with `Regs=[SecondDerivative/Laplacian]`, `epsRs=[...]` |\n| model best expressed in another basis | `preconditioned_inversion` with `P` (e.g. smoothing or a synthesis transform) |\n| sparse in the model or in a transform `T` (signal → coefficients) | `fista` (`SOp=T.H`) or `spgl1` (`SOp=T`, note the opposite convention) if a residual target `sigma` is known – see `pick-sparsifying-transform` |\n| few non-zeros, explicit dictionary | `omp` |\n| robust to outliers (L1 data misfit) | `irls` with `kind=\"data\"` |\n| blocky / TV-like, mixed L1 + L2 terms | `splitbregman` with `RegsL1=[FirstDerivative/Gradient]` |\n| constraints (bounds, positivity), TV with better control, other non-smooth terms | PyProximal: use the `pyproximal` plugin skill `solve-nonsmooth-problem` |\n\nAvoid `Op / y` in production code: it is a convenience wrapper with a fixed\n100 iterations and no control over stopping or regularisation.\n\nState which solver was picked and why (one or two sentences) before writing code.\n\n## 3. Write the script\n\nStart from `reference/inversion_template.py` and adapt it:\n\n- build (or import) the operator, load the data, reshape to `Op.dimsd`;\n- **scale** data and model sensibly: if `|y|` is ~1e-8 or ~1e8 normalise it and\n  undo the scaling on the result; badly scaled problems stall Krylov solvers;\n- set `x0` (zero, or a smooth background model when the user has one);\n- choose `niter` from the problem size and condition, not \"1000 to be safe\":\n  start with 20–100 for Krylov solvers and 100–500 for (F)ISTA, then look at the\n  cost curve. Use `tol` / `rtol` to stop early;\n- for regularised solvers, set initial weights from a scale argument\n  (e.g. `eps ≈ ||Op.H y|| / ||Reg.H Reg x||` order-of-magnitude) and mark them as\n  \"to be tuned\" – do not claim they are optimal;\n- for `fista`/`ista`, let `alpha=None` so PyLops estimates the step from the\n  largest eigenvalue, or pass `eigsdict={\"niter\": ..., \"tol\": ...}` for big\n  operators; `eps` is the threshold weight;\n- keep the whole solver return tuple and name its entries (they differ between\n  solvers – see `reference/solver_guide.md`);\n- save outputs (`np.save` / the project's I/O) rather than only plotting.\n\nPut the script where the user keeps analysis code (ask if ambiguous) and use\nthe project's plotting conventions if any.\n\n## 4. Check the result\n\nRun the script and report, with numbers:\n\n- solver exit status (`istop` where available) and iterations used;\n- the **cost curve** (log scale) – flat from iteration 1 means a wrong setup,\n  still decreasing at `niter` means increase it;\n- data residual `||y - Op x|| / ||y||` compared with the expected noise level\n  (much lower than the noise ⇒ overfitting; much higher ⇒ under-fitting or\n  a modelling error);\n- if the user has a true model (synthetic), `pylops.utils.metrics.snr(xtrue, xinv)`;\n- a plot of the model (and data, modelled data, residual).\n\nIf something looks wrong, switch to `debug-inversion` rather than randomly\nchanging parameters.\n\n## 5. Hand off\n\nReport: the solver and regularisation chosen and why, the file path, the\nconvergence summary above, and the parameters that should be tuned next\n(pointing to `tune-regularization`).\n"}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"dbd123d1-d66e-4ab0-aa94-85726fe79bd0","uuid":"4b636e0d-8a49-42c8-9039-095eea70f4e9","timestamp":"2026-11-01T21:12:29.970Z","isSynthetic":true}

Your data peak at about 1, so I didn't rescale them.\n2. **Main inversion:** I used `splitbregman` with a total-variation penalty (an L1 penalty on the first derivative). Your true signal is two flat boxes, and this penalty favours flat pieces separated by jumps, so edges stay sharp. Settings: `mu=1`, `epsRL1s=[0.1]`, 50 outer and 10 inner iterations.\n3. **Comparison:** I also ran `regularized_inversion` with a smoothness penalty (`SecondDerivative`, `eps=1`). This is the standard least-squares approach without a \"blocky\" assumption.\n\n**Results**\n\n| | Data misfit / noise level | SNR vs. true signal | Error vs. true signal |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| **TV (Split-Bregman)** | 0.91 | **32.1 dB** | **2.5%** |\n| Smooth (L2) | 0.93 | 14.4 dB | 19% |\n\n- **Data fit:** both methods fit the data to about the noise level (ratio close to 1), so neither is overfitting or underfitting. The leftover residual looks like random noise with no pattern.\n- **Convergence:** the Split-Bregman cost drops quickly and is flat after about 30 outer iterations, so 50 is enough. The least-squares solver behind the smooth method stopped normally after 147 iterations (`istop=2`).\n- **Shape of the result:** the TV result puts the edges at 40/80 and 120/150 and gets the levels 1.0 and −0.7. The smooth result blurs the edges and has overshoot and ringing near each jump (visible in the middle panel of `inversion_blur.png`).\n\n**Files** (in `/private/tmp/e-Yh6DiD/home/cwd/`)\n- `invert_blur.py`: the script. Settings can be changed from the command line, e.g. `python invert_blur.py --eps_tv 0.05 --mu 2`.\n- `xinv_tv.npy` and `xinv_l2.npy`: the two recovered signals.\n- `inversion_blur.png`: the data with the fitted data and residual, the true vs. recovered signals, and the cost curve.\n\n**Caveat:** I picked `mu`, `eps_tv` and `eps_l2` by reasoning about scale, not by a search. They aren't optimal, even though the fit sits near the noise level. (file state is current in your context — no need to Read it back)"}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"c7ce26b2-3325-444e-8000-4acdf223e0f4","uuid":"7f1c128f-06e9-466e-9fe5-66b6f51c2a6c","timestamp":"2026-11-01T21:13:43.249Z","tool_use_result":{"filePath":"/private/tmp/e-F8uPv6/home/cwd/deblur_inversion.py","oldString":"np.logspace(-3, -0.5, 15)","newString":"np.logspace(-3, 1, 21)","originalFile":"\"\"\"1-D deblurring with PyLops: naive LSQR vs Tikhonov vs Total Variation.\n\nRegularization weights are chosen with the discrepancy principle (residual norm\n~ sigma * sqrt(n), sigma = known noise std), NOT by comparing to xtrue, so the\nselection is something you can also do on real data. xtrue is only used at the\nend to report errors.\n\"\"\"\nimport numpy as np\nimport pylops\nfrom pylops.optimization.basic import lsqr\nfrom pylops.optimization.leastsquares import regularized_inversion\nfrom pylops.optimization.sparsity import splitbregman\n\n# ---------------- problem setup (as provided) ----------------\nrng = np.random.default_rng(5)\nn = 200\nz = np.arange(n)\nxtrue = np.zeros(n); xtrue[40:80] = 1.0; xtrue[120:150] = -0.7\nt = np.arange(-15, 16)\nh = np.exp(-0.5 * (t / 4) ** 2); h /= h.sum()\nOp = pylops.signalprocessing.Convolve1D(n, h=h, offset=15)\nsigma = 0.02\ny = Op @ xtrue + sigma * rng.standard_normal(n)\n\n# sanity: adjoint test\npylops.utils.dottest(Op, n, n, rtol=1e-6, raiseerror=True)\n\ntarget = sigma * np.sqrt(n)  # discrepancy-principle residual level\n\n\ndef rel_err(x):\n    return np.linalg.norm(x - xtrue) / np.linalg.norm(xtrue)\n\n\ndef resid(x):\n    return np.linalg.norm(y - Op @ x)\n\n\ndef pick_by_discrepancy(cands):\n    \"\"\"cands: list of (param, x). Largest param whose residual <= 1.05*target,\n    else the one with residual closest to target.\"\"\"\n    ok = [(p, x) for p, x in cands if resid(x) <= 1.05 * target]\n    if ok:\n        return max(ok, key=lambda c: c[0])\n    return min(cands, key=lambda c: abs(resid(c[1]) - target))\n\n\n# ---------------- 1) unregularized LSQR (many iterations) ----------------\nx_ls = lsqr(Op, y, x0=np.zeros(n), niter=500, damp=0.0)[0]\n\n# ---------------- 2) Tikhonov with first-derivative smoothing ----------------\nD1 = pylops.FirstDerivative(n, edge=True, kind=\"forward\")\ntik = []\nfor eps in np.logspace(-3, 0, 25):\n    x = regularized_inversion(Op, y, [D1], epsRs=[eps], x0=np.zeros(n),\n                              **dict(iter_lim=500, damp=0.0))[0]\n    tik.append((eps, x))\neps_tik, x_tik = pick_by_discrepancy(tik)\n\n# ---------------- 3) Total Variation via Split-Bregman ----------------\ntv = []\nfor eps in np.logspace(-3, -0.5, 15):\n    x = splitbregman(Op, y, [D1], niter_outer=60, niter_inner=5,\n                     mu=1.0, epsRL1s=[eps], tol=1e-6, tau=1.0,\n                     x0=np.zeros(n), **dict(iter_lim=30, damp=1e-10))[0]\n    tv.append((eps, x))\neps_tv, x_tv = pick_by_discrepancy(tv)\n\n# ---------------- report ----------------\nprint(f\"noise sigma={sigma}, discrepancy target ||y-Ax|| ~ {target:.3f}\\n\")\nprint(f\"{'method':<28}{'param':>10}{'||y-Ax||':>11}{'rel.err':>10}{'max|err|':>10}\")\nfor name, p, x in [(\"blurred data y (no inv.)\", np.nan, y),\n                   (\"LSQR, no regularization\", np.n

Total-variation (TV) regularization recovered your signal with about **3% relative error**, with sharp edges and correct block amplitudes.\n\n## What the script does\n1. **Setup and check:** It builds your operator and data exactly as you wrote them, then runs PyLops' `dottest` to confirm the operator and its adjoint match. They do.\n2. **Three inversions:**\n   - **Plain LSQR (no regularization):** a baseline to show why regularization is needed.\n   - **Tikhonov** (`regularized_inversion`) with a first-derivative penalty: a smooth, L2 prior.\n   - **TV** (`splitbregman`) with an L1 penalty on the first derivative. This prior favours piecewise-constant signals, which is what your `xtrue` is (two flat blocks).\n3. **Choosing the regularization weight:** I did **not** tune it against `xtrue`, since you won't have that on real data. I used the discrepancy principle instead: pick the strongest regularization whose data misfit ‖y − Ax‖ is still about σ·√n ≈ 0.283, using your noise level σ = 0.02. The first TV run landed on the top edge of my search range, so I widened the range and reran. Both final weights are now inside their ranges.\n\n## Results\n| Method | ‖y − Ax‖ | Relative error ‖x − xtrue‖/‖xtrue‖ | Max abs. error |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Blurred data `y` (no inversion) | 0.549 | 0.226 | 0.457 |\n| LSQR, no regularization | 0.180 | **243.8** (blows up) | 360 |\n| Tikhonov, eps = 0.56 | 0.280 | 0.194 | 0.449 |\n| **TV, eps = 0.40** | 0.290 | **0.029** | 0.096 |\n\nTV details:\n- **Block levels:** about 0.992 (true value 1.0) and −0.679 (true value −0.7).\n- **Background:** RMS of 0.009 outside the blocks.\n- **Edges:** sharp and in the right places at 40/80 and 120/150. The plot is in `deblur_inversion.png`.\n\n## What this shows\n- **No regularization fails badly.** The Gaussian blur almost wipes out high frequencies, so LSQR overfits the noise (its misfit drops below the noise level) and the solution blows up.\n- **Tikhonov is stable but barely better than the blurred data** (0.19 vs 0.23). Its smooth prior rounds off the edges and adds ringing next to the jumps, which you can see in the lower panel of the plot.\n- **TV fits this signal.** Its error is about 7× lower than Tikhonov's, and the remaining error is mostly a slight shrinkage of the block amplitudes (~1–3%), which is typical of L1 penalties.\n\n## Caveats\n- I used your known σ = 0.02 to choose the weights. On real data you'd need to estimate σ, or use an L-curve or cross-validation instead.\n- TV works this well because the true signal really is blocky. For a smooth signal, Tikhonov would be the better choice.\n\n## Two API details I had to fix along the way\n- `regularized_inversion` passes options to scipy's `lsqr`, so it takes `iter_lim=` rather than `niter=`.\n- `splitbregman` takes its arguments in the order `(Op, y, RegsL1, ...)`.\n\nRun it with `python deblur_inversion.py`. Unregularized least squares (LSQR, run to convergence)   -> shows noise blow-up\n  2. Tikhonov (first-derivative smoothing), lambda chosen by the discrepancy principle\n  3. Total variation (Split-Bregman), weight chosen by the discrepancy principle\n\nHyperparameters are chosen WITHOUT looking at xtrue: only the known noise level\n(sigma = 0.02) is used. xtrue is used only afterwards to report errors.\n\"\"\"\nimport numpy as np\nimport pylops\nfrom pylops.optimization.leastsquares import regularized_inversion\nfrom pylops.optimization.sparsity import splitbregman\n\n# ---------------------------------------------------------------- problem setup\nrng = np.random.default_rng(5)\nn = 200\nz = np.arange(n)\nxtrue = np.zeros(n); xtrue[40:80] = 1.0; xtrue[120:150] = -0.7\nt = np.arange(-15, 16)\nh = np.exp(-0.5 * (t / 4) ** 2); h /= h.sum()\nOp = pylops.signalprocessing.Convolve1D(n, h=h, offset=15)\nsigma = 0.02\ny = Op @ xtrue + sigma * rng.standard_normal(n)\n\n# Sanity check: operator passes the dot test (adjoint is consistent)\nassert pylops.utils.dottest(Op, n, n, rtol=1e-6)\n\ntarget_resid = sigma * np.sqrt(n)  # discrepancy principle: ||Op x - y|| ~ sigma*sqrt(n)\nD1 = pylops.FirstDerivative(n, edge=True, kind=\"forward\")\n\n\ndef relerr(x):\n    return np.linalg.norm(x - xtrue) / np.linalg.norm(xtrue)\n\n\ndef resid(x):\n    return np.linalg.norm(Op @ x - y)\n\n\ndef pick_by_discrepancy(lams, solve):\n    \"\"\"Largest lambda whose data residual is still <= target (Morozov).\"\"\"\n    results = [(lam, solve(lam)) for lam in lams]\n    ok = [(lam, x) for lam, x in results if resid(x) <= target_resid]\n    lam, x = max(ok, key=lambda p: p[0]) if ok else min(results, key=lambda p: resid(p[1]))\n    return lam, x, results\n\n\n# ---------------------------------------------------------------- 1. plain LSQR\nx_ls = pylops.optimization.basic.lsqr(Op, y, x0=np.zeros(n), niter=500, atol=0, btol=0)[0]\n\n# ---------------------------------------------------------------- 2. Tikhonov\ndef solve_tik(lam):\n    return regularized_inversion(Op, y, [D1], epsRs=[lam], iter_lim=500, atol=1e-10, btol=1e-10)[0]\n\nlams_tik = np.logspace(-3, 1, 41)\nlam_tik, x_tik, _ = pick_by_discrepancy(lams_tik, solve_tik)\n\n# ---------------------------------------------------------------- 3. Total variation\n# min_x 0.5||Op x - y||^2 + eps ||D1 x||_1   (Split-Bregman, mu = 1)\ndef solve_tv(eps):\n    return splitbregman(Op, y, [D1], niter_outer=60, niter_inner=5, mu=1.0,\n                        epsRL1s=[eps], tol=1e-6, tau=1.0, iter_lim=30, damp=1e-10)[0]\n\nlams_tv = np.logspace(-3, 0, 31)\nlam_tv, x_tv, _ = pick_by_discrepancy(lams_tv, solve_tv)\n\n# ---------------------------------------------------------------- report\nprint(f\"noise sigma = {sigma},  discrepancy target ||Ax-y|| = {target_resid:.4f}\")\nprint(f\"{'method':<28}{'param':>10}{'||Ax-y||':>12}{'rel. err':>12}\")\nfor name, p, x in [(\"LSQR (no regularization)\", np.nan, x_ls),\n                   (\"Tikhonov (D1, L2)\", lam_tik, x_tik),\n                   (\"Total variation (D1, L1)\", lam_tv, x_tv)]:\n    print(f\"{name:<28}{p:>10.4g}{resid(x):>12.4f}{relerr(x):>12.4f}\")\n\n# Recovered block amplitudes (interior of each block, away from edges)\nfor name, x in [(\"Tikhonov\", x_tik), (\"TV\", x_tv)]:\n    print(f\"{name:<9} mean x[45:75] = {x[45:75].mean():+.3f} (true +1.0), \"\n          f\"mean x[125:145] = {x[125:145].mean():+.3f} (true -0.7), \"\n          f\"max |x| off-support = {np.abs(np.r_[x[:35], x[85:115], x[155:]]).max():.3f}\")\n\n# ---------------------------------------------------------------- figure\ntry:\n    import matplotlib\n    matplotlib.use(\"Agg\")\n    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt\n\n    fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(9, 6), sharex=True)\n    axs[0].plot(z, xtrue, color=\"0.2\", lw=2, label=\"true x\")\n    axs[0].plot(z, y, color=\"0.6\", lw=1, label=\"blurred + noisy y\")\n    axs[0].set_title(\"Data\"); axs[0].legend(frameon=False)\n    axs[1].plot(z, xtrue, color=\"0.2\", lw=2, label=\"true x\")\n    axs[1].plot(z, x_tik, color=\"#1f77b4\", lw=1.5, label=f\"Tikhonov (err {relerr(x_tik):.2f})\")\n    axs[1].plot(z, x_tv, color=\"#d62728\", lw=1.5, label=f\"TV (err {relerr(x_tv):.2f})\")\n    axs[1].set_title(\"Inversions\"); axs[1].legend(frameon=False); axs[1].set_xlabel(\"z\")\n    for a in axs:\n        a.spines[[\"top\", \"right\"]].set_visible(False)\n    fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig(\"deblur_inversion.png\", dpi=120)\n    print(\"saved deblur_inversion.png\")\nexcept ImportError:\n    pass\n","structuredPatch":[],"originalFile":null,"userModified":false},"tool_result_meta":[{"id":"toolu_011vHgLZ2eGBozbfcjQ45o6u","permission_decision":{"decision":"accept","source":"config","reason_type":"rule"}

I have a 1-D blurring operator and noisy data, and I want to recover the underlying signal, but I have not written any inversion yet. Can you build the inversion for me? Here is how I generate the operator and the data:

import numpy as np
import pylops

rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
n = 200
z = np.arange(n)
xtrue = np.zeros(n); xtrue[40:80] = 1.0; xtrue[120:150] = -0.7
t = np.arange(-15, 16)
h = np.exp(-0.5 * (t / 4) ** 2); h /= h.sum()
Op = pylops.signalprocessing.Convolve1D(n, h=h, offset=15)
y = Op @ xtrue + 0.02 * rng.standard_normal(n)

Please write a runnable script, run it, and tell me what you did and how well it recovered the signal.
